newsitem.title: FRANCE: Farmers moan, but EU price cuts mask lack of reform.
newsitem.headline: Farmers moan, but EU price cuts mask lack of reform.

text.p: The European Union has effectively postponed radical farm reform, though attacks by its farmers and some capitals on plans for new price cuts to prepare for expansion eastwards tend to hide this fact, farm analysts said.

Proposals presented by the European Commission on Wednesday to cut dairy, cereal and beef support prices by up to 30 percent but only partly compensate farmers for income loss provoked a predictable barrage of protest in major farming countries, notably France and Germany.

But analysts said that farm spending, now some 30 percent higher than before the 1992 reform, will continue to defy gravity and that EU subsidies will be the focal point of attack in the next round of World Trade Organisation talks.
"There's no budgetary crisis to force real reform," Brian Gardner, an independent Brussels-based agriculture analyst, told Reuters.
But others said EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler's proposals represented a fine balance between the politically possible and the economically essential.

They added that farm ministers will find it more difficult than in the past to dilute the reforms after an EU summit in Amsterdam last month entrusted foreign ministers with the task of overseeing enlargement and spending plans.
Gardner warned however that by proposing higher production-linked compensatory payments to cereals and oilseed farmers, Fischler was building up problems in WTO negotiations starting in 1999.
The United States, the world's leading farm produce exporter which last year completely decoupled farm subsidies from production, is expected to lead the attack.
But Austria's Fischler, displaying typical Tyrolean stubbornness, has signalled he is ready to fight for the EU payments.
"It won't make life easy in the WTO but we are going to defend it," he said. "It's important we see that the measures are in the 'blue box' and within our obligations to the WTO."
The EU argues that the payments are based on historic reference yields, not current output, and respect WTO rules.
In Washington, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman welcomed the planned cut in crop support prices as a step towards more market-oriented policies but declined to prejudge the details.
U.S. agricultural experts, mindful of EU readiness to use export subsidies and taxes, were sceptical that the reforms would result in freer farm trade.
In Paris, French Farm Minister Louis le Pensec complained that voluntary price cuts ahead of talks could force the EU into making further concessions to its trade partners.

But the EU's executive argues that lowering farm prices will ease the integration of the eastern countries whose prices are much lower, reduce the risk of food mountains and keep spending under control.
Fischler noted that EU farmers had complained that Brussels was bowing to Washington's wishes and slashing subsidies.

Luc Guyau, the French leader of the EU farmers' lobby, COPA, representing eight million farmers, has warned that the reforms will result in a catastrophic cut in farmers' earnings and force many off the land.
In 1992, farmers took to the streets to protest against price cuts of five to 30 percent, but their worst fears proved unfounded and average incomes climbed 4.5 percent annually.

Analysts noted that despite severe financial curbs needed to meet criteria for economic and monetary union, agricultural expenditure was set to climb to 50 billion ecus ($54.9 billion) in 2006, from 43.3 billion in 1999.

Higher compensation payments will outweigh savings on export subsidies and market intervention to purchase surplus grain, beef and dairy products, resulting in a net increase in payouts of 4.0 billion ecus.
In addition some 2.1 billion ecus will be spent on creating new rural jobs and infrastructure schemes in the 15 EU countries by 2006.
Eastern European countries also stand to get 4.5 billion ecus of agricultural market and restructuring aid in 2006.
Commission officials said the increase reflected economic growth and was well within the spending ceiling. Without reform, food mountains would return and result in much higher costs.

Officials pointed out that if the previous GATT Uruguay Round was a guide, the WTO negotiations starting in 1999 were unlikely to reach crunch point until around 2005 when EU farm spending would also be up for review.

The Commission plans to start EU entry negotiations with a first wave of five eastern European countries -- Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Slovenia -- in early 1998 and hopes that they can start to join in 2002.

But analysts said this timetable could prove optimistic, given that it took Spain seven years to secure entry. Similarly it could be up to 10 years before the new members' farm products are freely traded throughout the EU.
"There's plenty of time before radical reform is unavoidable," said one of the many agricultural experts who converged on Strasbourg this week. ($ = 0.910 European Currency Unit ECUs)
